To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there was a strong association between increased macrolide resistance and the increased use of macrolide antibiotics in children in Slovenia.

the use of macrolide antibiotics decreased in Slovenia, but the rate of resistance of common respiratory bacteria increased, and that the use of intermediate acting macrolides was associated with increased resistance in children.

the use of macrolide antibiotics in the country decreased by 21%, from 3,81 DID in 1999 to DID in 2004, and resistance of common pathogens, Streptococcus pneumonie, Streptococous pyogenes, Haemophilus influenze, and Moraxella cattarhalis, increased during this period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between antibiotic consumption and antibiotic resistance.
the impact of macrolide consumption on resistance of S. pneumonia and S. pyogenis.
the relationship between macrolide consumption and resistance in common respiratory pathogens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reduction of macrolides use in Slovenia was not followed by a decrease in resistance of S. pneumonia, but by a rise in resistance rates.
there is a need to decrease the consumption of macrotides in children and adults, especially in the case of the intermediate acting ones.
the reduction of macrolide use did not lead to a decrease of macrolide resistance in respiratory pathogens in children and adults in Slovenia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
macrolides should not be used for prophylaxis of acute otitis media in children and should not be used empirically for community-acquired pneumonia in adults.
there is a need for a more rational use of antibiotics in Slovenia.
the decline in total macrole use was not paralleleled by reduced macrole resistance rates of Streptococus pyogenes and Streptococus pneumoniae during 6-year period.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the decline in total macromolecule consumption was not accompanied by a decrease in macromolecule resistance rates for S. pyogens and S. pneumonia in children and adults during the 6 years of the study.
the reduction of macrolide use in Slovenia was not followed by reduced macrolides resistance rates.
the reduction in macrolide use in Slovenia was not paralleled with reduced macrolide-resistance rates of Streptococci in children and adults.
